item.title: If you can't explain something in simple terms, you don't understand it (2017)
item.description:
Source: kottke.org

Top Comment:

I think this idea is often misunderstood and used as an excuse by people who don’t want to make any effort to understand a complex concept and want to blame the results of their laziness on the explanation or the explainer.

There are things where you may be given an explanation in simple terms, but the concept requires effort on the part of the recipient of the explanation to really understand. I’ll give an example: compactness. Probably anyone who has done analysis is familiar with how this concept is usually taught. Typically how it goes is you do open and closed sets and then they hit you with “a set is compact if and only if every open cover has a finite subcover”. Now this definition is extremely profound but very dense and it’s highly non-obvious why that in particular is the property you want (a finite subcover for every open cover)[1], how you could go about proving that every possible open cover in a certain situation could have a finite subcover etc etc.

In this case it’s actually quite easy to give simple explanations of the separate parts of the definition (open and closed sets, what an open cover therefore means, what a finite subcover then is etc) but actually understanding the concept of compactness requires something above and beyond whatever explanation you are given: it requires the reader to get out pencil and paper, try out some sets, go for some walks, think about it in the bath etc.

You may get a really fantastic explanation in simple terms from someone who deeply understands the topic, but if you don’t put in the effort you’re not going to understand it yourself. That’s not the fault of the explanation. It’s not an easy concept to grasp so you have to climb the ladder of understanding. The explainer can’t do that for you.

[1] it took the mathematical community years to settle on this being the definition, so you shouldn’t expect to understand why this is the definition straight away.

item.title: "I can tell you wrote this yourself"
item.description:
Source: em-online.bearblog.dev

Top Comment:

AI and LLMs, in my opinion, are effectively the industrialization of knowledge work.

Like it or not, industrialization brought many benefits and we couldn't imagine our modern way of living without it (just think about medicines). Industrial production made so many things so much more accessible for so many people.

But an industrialist perspective doesn't care about the process of making stuff, only about the outcome. The shoemakers deep knowledge of leathers, his intuition of all sorts of different shoes, and the pride of that competence—that doesn't matter when you can make thousands of shoes a day that cost 0.5% of something artisanal. The people working at the shoe factory only carry things to and fro and occasionally fix some machine issue.

This has tons of benefits and tons of downsides. But with physical goods, a shoe is a shoe.

With knowledge work like writing, the process is often the entire point. The point of writing a paper is what you learned in the process. The point of documented software architecture is to develop an understanding deep enough to drive coherent downstream decisions. If those things are no longer true, the asset it stands for is basically worthless.

item.title: PostgreSQL 19
item.description:
Source: www.postgresql.org

Top Comment:

Amazing release, really exciting features:

- REPACK CONCURRENTLY to reclaim disk space, which also affects performance.

- Logical replication of sequences - Fantastic addition. This is a missing piece in the major-version upgrade story which required extra scripting, and enable additional usecases.

- WAIT FOR LSN is a game-changer for read-replicas. For read-after-write, where the write goes to the master and the read hits a random replica. And also read-after-read, where each read may hit different replicas.

Add to that additional performance improvement and the plan advice extension, this makes 19 one of the most exciting releases of PostgreSQL.

Big big big kudos to the contributors, thank you!

item.title: OpenSSL: Buffer overflow in EVP_EncodeBlock() (CVE-2026-121481, CVSS 9.8)
item.description:
Source: github.com

Top Comment:

On a very very quick read, the bug is that EVP_EncodeBlock malfunctions if the input is larger than ~1.5GB. EVP_EncodeBlock is a function that encodes base64.

https://docs.openssl.org/1.0.2/man3/EVP_EncodeInit/

As a seasoned C programmer, I can immediately observe that the whole API is bad: the caller is expected to calculate the buffer length on their own, using a nontrivial formula, and the caller does not pass in the output buffer length, so the implementation cannot validate it. But apparently OpenSSL 4 also implemented it wrong and wrote (possibly far) past the end of the buffer.

You should probably assume that, if you are running anything that can be convinced to use this API to encode a very long blob as base64, then you are in trouble. I don’t know why a modern server would do this.

BTW, OpenSSL seems to be a rather low quality implementation of a very low quality set of APIs. Stay away.

edit: Fixed my size threshold, hopefully. I was thinking of unsigned ints, but this is a signed int. I have not looked at the code, just the description.

item.description:
Source: terrytao.wordpress.com

Top Comment:

Something I don’t quite know, maybe someone closer to math can answer this question

It seems we’re making tremendous progress on the back of existing abstractions and concepts with the brute force ability to generate language and verify proofs.

For example, Tao says about the Riemann proof:

> appears to use the full power of modern developments on the Langlands program and arithmetic geometry

What I wonder: how do we create new abstractions and concepts? Like whatever “Langlands program” is? That then feedback into the system, and allow for even more sophisticated mathematics.

Are we assuming AI will do this? Or does this still need to be something at least agreed-upon by a mathematics community - in the same way programmers talk about a “linked list” without having an hour long conversation to define it axiomatically? And without that social aspect, without breaking down long proofs into Lego block common abstractions, math may plateau? In part because we lose the ability to ask meaningful questions?
